problemSolved: A scroll-scrubbed multi-scene film needs a single flat timeline (scroll position -> which clip, and how far into it) built from a designer's per-section config, without the designer hand-computing pixel ranges.
mechanism: Builds a flat `SEGMENTS` array by walking `SECTIONS` and interleaving a `dive` segment per section with an optional `conn` (connector) segment between consecutive sections (skipped when `connectors[i]` is falsy, so a missing asset degrades gracefully instead of breaking the chain). Each segment carries a scroll-width weight (`w`); layout() later turns weights into cumulative pixel start/end offsets.
whyItWorks: Decouples 'what media exists and in what order' (a designer-editable config) from 'how much total scroll height that requires' (computed) and from 'what is currently active' (derived every scroll tick) — three concerns that would otherwise tangle into one hard-coded pixel table.
requiredContext: a config object with an ordered `sections` array and an optional `connectors` array of equal-or-shorter length
outputImpact: This is the load-bearing data structure the entire engine reads from (layout, read, raf all iterate `SEGMENTS`) — get this wrong and nothing else in the file matters.
failureModes: No validation that `connectors.length === sections.length - 1`; a mismatched array silently misaligns which connector sits between which two scenes.
testMethod: No automated test exists in the repo (see TESTING.md); correctness is implied by the rest of the engine working, not separately verified.
sitesmithForm: Reuse this data shape verbatim for any SiteSmith scroll-scrubbed hero: an ordered scene array with optional connector/transition slots between them, converted to a flat weighted timeline at layout time — independent of whether the underlying clips are AI-generated, stock, or client-supplied.

problemSolved: Setting `video.currentTime` from scroll position ("scrubbing") silently fails on hosts that don't serve HTTP byte-range requests (including `python -m http.server`): `video.seekable` pins to `[0,0]` and every seek clamps to frame 0, so the clip looks frozen no matter how it was encoded.
mechanism: `loadClip()` fetches each clip with `fetch(url).then(r => r.blob())` and plays it from `URL.createObjectURL(blob)` instead of pointing `<video src>` directly at the network URL. A `Blob`-backed video is always fully seekable regardless of the origin server's range support.
whyItWorks: It sidesteps the actual failure mode (server byte-range support) entirely by making the browser scrub an in-memory object instead of a network resource — a root-cause fix, not a workaround for symptoms, and it is the stated reason the engine does not need all-intra encoding (SKILL.md:533-534).
requiredContext: none beyond the clip URL being fetchable (same-origin or CORS-permitting)
outputImpact: Without this, the entire premise of the skill (scroll-scrubbed video) breaks on a large class of static hosts. This is the single fix most responsible for the feature working at all outside a CDN with range support.
failureModes: Loads the whole clip into memory before it's scrubbable — fine for the ~1-8s clips this skill targets, would not scale to long-form video without chunked loading.

No retry/backoff on fetch failure beyond a silent `.catch(() => { s.loading = false })`, so a transient network blip permanently skips that clip for the session unless the user re-triggers `loadClip` by re-entering its scroll range.
testMethod: Asserted only in the source (no automated test); it is a well-known, independently verifiable browser behavior (Blob URLs are always seekable) rather than something specific to this codebase.
sitesmithForm: Standard technique for any SiteSmith build that scrubs video by scroll position, regardless of asset source — fetch-to-blob before scrubbing, and treat static-host byte-range gaps as the default assumption rather than an edge case.

problemSolved: Even with frame-matched clip boundaries, an instantaneous cut between two `<video>` elements at a segment boundary reads as a pop; adjacent scenes need to visually hand off rather than snap.
mechanism: For every segment, `read()` computes `outside` (pixel distance from the current scroll position to that segment's start/end) and maps it through `smooth(1 - outside/fade)` (a smoothstep) to set `opacity` and `z-index`, so segments overlap-fade over a configurable `CROSSFADE` band (default 0.12 viewport-heights) around each seam rather than switching visibility in one frame.
whyItWorks: A short cross-dissolve masks small residual mismatch at a seam (the source notes even frame-matched Seedance/Monid output lands within ~PSNR 27-31 dB, not pixel-perfect) without requiring perfect asset continuity — the crossfade and the frame-matching are complementary, not either/or (SKILL.md:516-519).
requiredContext: scroll position, segment start/end offsets from the layout pass
outputImpact: Directly determines whether scene transitions look 'connected' or 'cut' — the visible signature of the whole product.
failureModes: Purely a media-agnostic dissolve; it has no awareness of *content* similarity between the two overlapping frames, so it will just as happily paper over a genuinely mismatched pair of clips as a well-matched one — it's not a substitute for actually matching content, only for masking small residual drift.
testMethod: None automated; verification is by eye per SKILL.md Step 8 (screenshot before/after each seam).
sitesmithForm: Reusable as a generic 'any two adjacent scroll-bound media segments cross-dissolve over N vh at their shared boundary' rule for SiteSmith scroll-driven sections, independent of what the media is.

problemSolved: A linear scroll-to-time mapping makes the camera move at constant perceived speed through a scene, so there's no way to make the copy's peak moment (e.g. the headline) coincide with the visual moment that best supports it.
mechanism: `lingerEase(x, L)` is a monotone remap: `(1-L)*x + L*(4*c^3 + 0.5)` where `c = x-0.5`, with `L` clamped 0..1. At `L=0` it's identity (linear); as `L` rises it flattens the middle of the range (camera settles) and steepens the edges (camera moves faster near seams) while preserving `f(0)=0` and `f(1)=1` exactly, so seam frames are never touched by the remap.
whyItWorks: It's a single-parameter, per-section dial that changes pacing without touching the underlying clip or the seam-continuity guarantee — a designer can make the hero scene 'linger' at its best frame just by setting one number, no re-render needed.
outputImpact: Medium — a pacing/craft refinement, not a correctness fix; makes the difference between a mechanically uniform scroll and one that feels directed.
failureModes: `L` close to 1 ('full pause') combined with a short scroll distance can make the scene feel stuck rather than deliberate — the source itself recommends keeping `L <= 0.6` (scrub-engine.js:23) but does not enforce it.
sitesmithForm: Reusable as-is: a cubic-ease time remap with a single 0-1 'linger' parameter per scroll-bound section, guaranteed boundary-preserving, for any SiteSmith build with scroll-driven pacing (video or otherwise, e.g. staged reveal of content blocks).

problemSolved: Scroll-scrubbed video has several distinct, well-known phone failure modes that each need a separate fix: fast flicks pile up seeks and freeze the decoder; iOS Safari won't paint a seeked frame on a muted video that was never played; the URL bar collapsing fires a `resize` that re-runs layout and yanks scroll position; and a heavier decode budget than desktop.
mechanism: Four independent fixes bundled behind one `isMobile()` check (coarse pointer OR <=860px, `scrub-engine.js:71-73`): (1) seek-coalescing — `raf()` skips re-queuing `currentTime` while `video.seeking` is still true (`276-286`); (2) iOS priming — a muted `play()->pause()` on first touch gesture plus keeping the still poster visible until the video's `seeked` event actually fires, not just `loadedmetadata` (`212-220,291-307`); (3) resize gating — `onResize()` ignores height-only changes on touch and only relayouts on an actual width change, leaving `orientationchange` as the separate rotation path (`317-320`); (4) a coarser seek epsilon on mobile (`0.02` vs `0.008`, line 274) to reduce decode churn.
whyItWorks: Each fix targets one concrete, named bug rather than a general 'make it faster' effort, so each is independently testable and independently removable — the four are documented as a matched set in `SKILL.md` Gotchas (frozen/blank video, phone-stutter, page-jump entries, lines 685-696) rather than left implicit.
requiredContext: a coarse-pointer/viewport-width check computed once at mount plus live width tracking
outputImpact: High for any mobile visitor — without this bundle the same engine that works on desktop reliably breaks on iOS Safari and stutters on mid-range Android, per the Gotchas list's own framing.
failureModes: The `coarse` pointer check is captured once at mount and never re-evaluated (comment at line 68-70 acknowledges this is intentional, since input type doesn't change mid-session) — a device that changes pointer type mid-session (rare, e.g. plugging in a mouse to a tablet) would not be caught.
testMethod: None automated; the source recommends manual QA with CPU throttling and real-device iOS Safari testing (SKILL.md:630-636).
sitesmithForm: Adopt all four fixes as a standard checklist for any SiteSmith scroll-video build: seek-coalescing, poster-until-seeked + first-touch priming, width-only resize gating, coarser mobile seek epsilon — each is small, independently verifiable, and has no dependency on how the video was produced.

problemSolved: A user with `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` set should not receive scrubbed video motion at all, but a naive implementation might just disable the scroll listener while still downloading and half-rendering video.
mechanism: `reduce` is read once at mount (`matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)')`) and `loadClip()` short-circuits immediately if `reduce` is true — clips are never fetched, never decoded; only the still images remain, and they simply cross-dissolve via the same opacity math used for seams. The CSS also disables the scroll-hint wheel animation and hides particles under the same media query.
whyItWorks: It's a full degrade at the data-fetching layer, not a cosmetic override at the rendering layer — no wasted bandwidth or decode cost for a user who will never see the motion, and the fallback (still-image cross-dissolve) reuses existing code paths instead of a separate branch.
outputImpact: Directly satisfies a real accessibility requirement and, as a side effect, is the only fully-graceful path when video assets are entirely unavailable (no credits, no backend) — the same code path could be forced on for a build with zero video.
failureModes: Only triggers on the OS-level reduced-motion preference; there's no separate opt-in for a user who wants a lightweight/no-video experience for other reasons (bandwidth, low-end device) without also having reduced-motion set at the OS level.
testMethod: None automated in this repo; testable by toggling the OS/browser setting and confirming no video request fires.
sitesmithForm: Reuse the pattern generally: gate any generated/heavy media fetch behind the same check used to gate its motion, so accessibility and 'no backend available' degrade through one code path instead of two.

problemSolved: A component that injects its own default CSS custom properties needs a page's own `:root`/theme rules to win, without the component author having to predict every selector the host page might use or resorting to `!important`.
mechanism: The engine's injected stylesheet is wrapped in `@layer sw { … }`. Because unlayered CSS (ordinary page rules, including a page's own `:root`/`.sw-root { --sw-bg: … }` block) always outranks any `@layer`-wrapped CSS in the cascade regardless of selector specificity or injection order, the host page's theme tokens win automatically.
whyItWorks: This is a native platform feature doing exactly what a specificity hack or `!important` would otherwise be reached for, with none of the fragility — order-independent and future-proof against however the component's own CSS grows.
requiredContext: a browser supporting CSS `@layer` (broadly supported in evergreen browsers)
outputImpact: Small mechanism, but removes an entire class of theming bugs (host page can't override an injected component's defaults) for near-zero cost.
failureModes: No fallback noted for browsers without `@layer` support — on those, the component's unlayered defaults would compete on ordinary specificity/order rules instead, which the source does not address.
testMethod: None automated; a straightforward CSS-cascade fact, verifiable by inspecting the compiled stylesheet.
sitesmithForm: Standard technique for any SiteSmith-authored component/widget that ships default CSS custom properties meant to be overridden by a host page: wrap the component's own defaults in `@layer`, leave the page's theme rules unlayered.

problemSolved: Naive assumptions about what makes video scrub smoothly are backwards: teams reach for all-intra encoding (huge files) or downscale quality, when the actual lever is seekability (solved by blob-loading, not encoding) and keyframe distance from the decoder's perspective.
mechanism: Documents a concrete encode recipe independent of the clip's origin: native resolution (never upscale/downscale for the sake of seeking), `crf ~20`, small GOP (`-g 8`, not all-intra — all-intra bloats an 8s clip to ~25 MB vs ~8 MB at GOP 8), stripped audio, `+faststart`, light `unsharp` to counter video-vs-still softness. A separate, tighter mobile profile (`-g 4`, 720p, crf 23) trades a few more keyframes for cheaper phone-decoder seeks, since seek cost scales with frames-from-nearest-keyframe on weaker hardware.
whyItWorks: Ties every setting to a stated, checkable cause (GOP size -> decode cost per seek; blob-loading -> seekability; crf/unsharp -> perceived quality vs file size) rather than folklore ('all-intra is safest'), and gives two calibrated presets (desktop/mobile) instead of one compromise setting.
requiredContext: ffmpeg on PATH; any source video (generated or not)
outputImpact: Directly determines whether a scroll-scrubbed video feels smooth or stutters/bloats, on both desktop and mobile.
failureModes: The recipe is tuned for short clips (5-10s); the source does not claim it holds for longer-form scrubbed video, where GOP-8 file size savings would compound differently.
testMethod: None automated in-repo; verifiable by encoding a test clip and profiling seek latency, which the source does not itself do (asserted from experience, not measured in this codebase).
sitesmithForm: Carry this recipe as reference documentation for any SiteSmith scroll-video build, regardless of asset source: blob-load for seekability, GOP 8 desktop / GOP 4 mobile, native resolution, crf 20-23, no audio, faststart.

sourcePath: skills/scroll-world/SKILL.md:752-762 (References section) and file structure under references/
problemSolved: A procedure with heavy reference material (every prompt template, every batch script) would bloat the main entry point if inlined, costing context on every invocation even for steps the build never reaches.
mechanism: `SKILL.md` is the only file always loaded; it names `references/prompts.md`, `references/pipeline.md`, `references/scrub-engine.js`, `references/index-template.html`, and `references/knockout.py` by relative path at the exact step each is needed, and a closing References section restates what each file is for. None of the reference files is read unless that step is reached (e.g. `knockout.py` is optional and only relevant to Step 3).
whyItWorks: Matches the general skill-authoring principle that a procedure and its heavy reference data should be separate files loaded on demand — the same shape SiteSmith's own `SKILL.md` size limit (500 lines, CI-enforced per this project's CLAUDE.md) implicitly assumes.
requiredContext: an agent runtime that can read a named file mid-procedure (true for Claude Code / Codex)
outputImpact: Keeps the always-loaded cost to the 762-line `SKILL.md` rather than the full 1,686-line combined total of `SKILL.md` + the four text/JS reference files — real, but the base cost is still large relative to the proven 55-line/2078-token winner (see CONTEXT-STRATEGY.md).
failureModes: The split is undermined in practice: SKILL.md itself still inlines large vendor-specific tables that arguably belong in a reference file (the render-tier/Monid-pricing table at SKILL.md:156-198, the full model-capability table at SKILL.md:286-297, and the Monid backend section at SKILL.md:324-367 together add ~150 lines of always-loaded pricing/schema detail to the entry point).
testMethod: Verified directly by reading SKILL.md and confirming each reference file is named only at its point of use, and by line-counting what's inlined vs deferred.
sitesmithForm: Keep the pattern (procedure file names reference files by relative path at point of use, nothing pre-loaded) but apply it more strictly than this source does: move any vendor-pricing-table or model-capability-table content out of the main SKILL.md and into a reference file, since those are exactly the kind of heavy, rarely-needed detail progressive disclosure exists to defer.

problemSolved: Presenting a made-up multiple-choice list of industries/subjects at intake biases the user toward the options shown and reads as the assistant deciding the user's business for them, rather than letting them state it in their own words.
mechanism: Explicitly instructs asking the subject as an open plain-prose question ('What should this world be about?') and reserves `AskUserQuestion`/structured multiple-choice for the genuinely enumerable, lower-stakes choices later in the interview (art direction, camera style, brand-kit approach) — and even there, to signal an 'Other' escape hatch.
whyItWorks: It's a reasoning/prompting instruction to the model about *when* structured choice helps versus when it constrains — the same category of mechanism the frontend-design skill's winning file uses (guide the model's judgment with prose, don't move the decision into a fixed list) rather than a script or lookup table.
outputImpact: Medium — affects the quality of the very first interaction in a build; a biased subject-intake question would propagate through everything downstream.
failureModes: No mechanism verifies the model actually asked openly rather than defaulting to a menu anyway under time pressure — it's a norm, not a checkpoint.
sitesmithForm: Extract the general rule, not the video-specific content: in SiteSmith's own client-interview/direction-setting step, ask identity-defining questions (what is this business, what is it for) as open prose, and reserve structured multiple-choice only for genuinely enumerable, lower-stakes decisions (e.g. light/dark default, a short list of layout archetypes) — always with an explicit 'or describe your own' option.

problemSolved: Silently substituting a similar-sounding but incompatible tool/model for a user's stated preference produces a broken result (here: a video model that can't accept an end-image can't make a connector, so the seam law simply fails) without ever telling the user why.
mechanism: States the selection rule as a hard capability check ('the only usable models are ones that can frame-lock a seam... check with `higgsfield model get <job_type>`') and explicitly directs declining a user's out-of-roster model request with a one-line reason rather than substituting a roster model silently.
whyItWorks: Fail-loud-with-reason beats silent substitution or silent failure — the user gets to make an informed choice (accept the constraint, or accept a different, correctly-communicated trade-off) instead of receiving an inexplicably degraded result.
requiredContext: a way to introspect the chosen tool/model's actual capability contract before depending on it
outputImpact: Prevents a specific, otherwise-silent class of broken output (missing connectors) but only fires when a user requests something out-of-roster — low frequency, meaningful when it happens.
failureModes: Entirely dependent on a capability-introspection command existing for the tool in question (`higgsfield model get`); the general principle has no teeth without an equivalent check for whatever SiteSmith is verifying.
testMethod: Asserted only; no automated check in-repo confirms this rule is followed rather than just documented.
sitesmithForm: General engineering discipline worth carrying, not a discrete feature: before committing a build decision to a library/API/font/model choice the user requested, verify it actually supports what the plan needs and say so explicitly if it doesn't, rather than quietly picking something else. Low priority to formalize as its own SiteSmith mechanism since it's closer to baseline engineering practice than a novel technique.

problemSolved: Metered, real-money generation (image/video gens billed per clip) needs the user's informed consent on cost before anything renders, especially since a mid-run failure ('not_enough_credits') is recoverable but ugly.
mechanism: Presents render tiers with a cost table, computes an estimated total from the user's actual scene count and mobile choice (`N stills + (2N-1) videos, x2 if mobile, +15% re-roll headroom`), calibrates against a live balance check rather than guessing, and requires an explicit go-ahead before generating.
whyItWorks: It's a real-money spend gate: state the number, get consent, then act — a sound pattern wherever an action has an irreversible, metered cost.
requiredContext: a billed backend with an inspectable balance/pricing API
outputImpact: High stakes when applicable (protects the user from surprise spend) but zero relevance to a build with no metered backend.
failureModes: No analogue at all when there is no paid, metered generation step in the build — the entire mechanism is inert.
conflicts: Directly conflicts with the premise that SiteSmith's build step (current state, per project context) does not call a metered paid-generation backend — there is nothing for this gate to protect against today.
sitesmithForm: No coherent role in SiteSmith as it stands: SiteSmith's build step doesn't spend metered money, so there is no cost to gate. Revisit only if SiteSmith wires in a paid generation backend (e.g. an image-gen API) as a build-time dependency — at that point, adopt the shape (stated estimate, live balance check, explicit consent) rather than reinventing it.

problemSolved: Two independently-generated video clips that are supposed to connect (e.g. a dive into scene i and a connector into scene i+1) will not visually match, because every generation of the same subject renders slightly differently.
mechanism: Requires that a connector's `--start-image`/`--end-image` be the ACTUAL last/first frame extracted (via `ffmpeg`) from the already-rendered neighbouring clips, never the original source still — so `dive_i.end == connector.start` and `connector.end == dive_{i+1}.start` are frame-identical by construction, not by luck.
whyItWorks: It's a real, generalizable idea (condition the next generation on your own actual prior output, not the original prompt input, to prevent drift across a generative chain) but it only has a mechanism to act on when there is a generative step in the loop with start/end-image conditioning support.
requiredContext: a video-generation backend that accepts image conditioning on both ends of a clip
outputImpact: This is the single rule the source calls out as the difference between a connected world and a visibly cut one (SKILL.md:32-35) — but entirely inside the paid-pipeline half.
failureModes: Zero applicability without a generative video backend: there is no 'next frame' to extract when clips are not being generated in a chain to begin with (e.g. stock footage, client-supplied video) — the problem this solves doesn't exist in that context.
conflicts: Conflicts with SiteSmith's current scope: SiteSmith has no generative video backend, so there is no chain to keep frame-identical.
testMethod: Manual screenshot diffing per SKILL.md Step 8; no automated frame-comparison tool ships in the repo.
sitesmithForm: Not applicable to SiteSmith today — no generative video backend exists to chain. The underlying idea (condition on your own actual output, not the original input, to prevent drift across generation steps) is worth remembering in the abstract but has no concrete SiteSmith use case to attach to right now.

problemSolved: Frames itself as solving 'how do we make a cohesive, non-generic world' by fixing the art direction and camera behavior to a small enumerated set (clay diorama / papercraft / glossy toy / claymation / neon-night styles; fly-through / walkthrough / locked-iso camera architectures) reused verbatim across every build.
mechanism: A shared 'style preamble' is composed once at intake and then reused byte-for-byte in every scene-still prompt for cohesion (`prompts.md:3-4,33-43`); camera behavior is likewise selected once from a 3-way enumerated roster and applied uniformly for the whole film.
whyItWorks: Internally consistent (it is genuinely why the individual scenes of one build look cohesive with each other) but the mechanism that produces per-build cohesion is the same kind of mechanism that produces cross-build sameness: a small fixed menu of looks, reused verbatim, is precisely the shape of thing our own three-site convergence test (showcase 0/8) flagged as a liability, just operating at the level of one narrow genre (scroll-cinematic diorama sites) instead of across SiteSmith's whole output.
requiredContext: the shared style preamble and chosen camera architecture, held fixed for the whole build
outputImpact: High within a single build (this is why one build's scenes look like one world) but the same property is a house-style risk if this skill's aesthetic became SiteSmith's default answer to 'scroll storytelling' rather than one of many possible treatments a model reasons its own way into per-brief.
failureModes: Every scroll-world build necessarily looks like a member of the same small family (clay-diorama-isometric, or one of four listed alternates) by design — there is no mechanism here for the model to invent a genuinely novel visual treatment per subject the way frontend-design's subject-grounding-mandate pushes for.
Two unrelated businesses both choosing 'fly-through' + default clay-diorama style would converge on visually similar sites for reasons structural to this mechanism, not coincidence.
conflicts: Directly in tension with the measured fact that a fixed-look mechanism is a liability even when each individual output is good (three-site convergence, showcase 0/8).
testMethod: Not tested for cross-build convergence in the source; would require the same kind of multi-brief comparison SiteSmith itself already ran.
sitesmithForm: Do not adopt the fixed style-roster shape as a general SiteSmith mechanism. If a scroll-cinematic capability is ever offered, treat art direction and camera behavior as brief-driven creative decisions the model reasons about per project (in the spirit of frontend-design's subject-grounding), not a menu of five preset looks reused across builds.

problemSolved: Removing a flat, solid background from a generated still (to let a diorama 'float' over an atmospheric page background) while preserving interior regions that happen to match the background colour (e.g. cream interior walls) — a plain global colour-key would wrongly punch through those too.
mechanism: Samples the four corner pixels as the background colour, then flood-fills from the image border inward (BFS over a visited/background bitmask) marking only border-connected pixels within an RGB-distance tolerance as background, so any same-colour region not connected to the border survives; the resulting alpha mask gets a small Gaussian blur to soften the cutout edge.
whyItWorks: Border-connectivity is the correct constraint for this exact scenario (all AI-generated stills in this pipeline share the same 'floating island on solid background' framing) — it is a small, correct, narrowly-scoped algorithm, not a general-purpose background remover (it would not handle a photo with a genuinely irregular background touching the subject).
outputImpact: Cosmetic-only (the 'floating diorama' look), and explicitly optional in the source itself (Step 3: 'if you'd rather keep it simple, just match the page background colour and skip this').
failureModes: Tolerance-based colour matching (`TOL=34` RGB distance) can eat into subject pixels that happen to be near the background colour (e.g. a light-coloured subject edge) with no protection beyond the blur softening the boundary.
Assumes a genuinely flat corner-sampled background; fails silently (wrong knockout) on a still with any background gradient or texture.
testMethod: None automated; visual inspection only, per the source's own instruction to 'review the stills' generally.
sitesmithForm: No current SiteSmith use case: this utility exists specifically to serve the AI-diorama pipeline's own visual convention (solid-bg floating islands), which SiteSmith is not adopting. Revisit only if a specific SiteSmith feature needs solid-background image cutout as a standalone step — at that point this border-flood-fill approach (rather than a naive global colour-key) is the right algorithm to reach for.
